item.title: SpaceX’s Musk says Tesla merger good idea but far from certain, needs 50% of Tesla shares
item.description:
The merger remark is likely to draw the most attention, particularly for Tesla shareholders, though Musk’s own caveats suggest it is an idea rather than a plan, which may limit any sustained move. Requiring approval from half of all Tesla shares sets a high bar, so investors may treat the comment as a long-dated possibility rather than a near-term catalyst. The compute comments are a cleaner read-through: a claim that older Nvidia H100 chips now rent for more than when new points to tight supply across AI infrastructure, which would tend to support sentiment toward Nvidia, server makers and AI cloud providers. Coming on the same session as Super Micro’s surprise upgrade, it adds to a run of strong AI demand signals.

Musk floated a SpaceX-Tesla merger while stressing it may never happen, but his clearer message was that AI compute remains so scarce that even older chips are rising in value.

Summary:

  • SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on the company’s earnings call that a merger with Tesla would be a good idea but is far from certain
  • He said any deal would need shareholder support, including approval from 50% of all Tesla shares
  • Musk said demand for AI compute is likely to remain strong
  • He said older Nvidia H100 chips are now renting for more than when they were new
  • He warned a shortage of compute for superintelligence could persist for a long time
  • The comments follow SpaceX’s quarterly results, in which AI revenue beat forecasts and made up more than half of sales

More from SpaceX’s earnings call, where chief executive Elon Musk said a merger between SpaceX and Tesla would be a good idea but cautioned that it is far from certain, while also signalling that demand for AI computing power shows no sign of easing.

Musk said any combination would require shareholder support, including approval from 50% of all Tesla shares. The reference to all shares suggests a threshold based on total shares outstanding rather than only those voted, which would set a considerably higher bar. He gave no indication of a proposal, a timetable or any formal talks, and his comments are best read as a view on a possible future structure rather than a deal in progress.

On AI, Musk said demand for compute is likely to remain strong. He said older Nvidia H100 chips are currently renting for more than they did when new, a sign, in his view, of how tight the supply of AI processing capacity has become. He also warned that a shortage of the compute needed to develop superintelligence could last for a long time.

The comments add context to SpaceX’s third-quarter results, released earlier in the session. Revenue of about $14.6 billion beat forecasts, with the AI segment contributing about $7.6 billion, or more than half the total. Capital spending of about $19.6 billion, most of it directed at AI, exceeded quarterly revenue, so Musk’s view that compute will stay scarce helps explain why the company continues to invest at that pace.

The remarks also landed on the same day Super Micro Computer released a surprise preliminary update showing September-quarter revenue well ahead of its own guidance, adding to evidence that spending on AI infrastructure remains robust.

For now, the merger idea looks like a long-term possibility with significant hurdles, while the compute message is more immediately relevant for investors tracking the AI hardware trade. Any further detail from Musk or either company on the merger would be the next thing to watch.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS flags 3 tests for the AI trade as Meta kicks off mega-cap tech earnings
item.description:
With rates rising and financing costs higher, the tolerance for open-ended AI spending is narrowing, which puts capex guidance at the centre of market reaction this season. Any sign that spending is outpacing revenue could hit hyperscaler shares even on headline beats, while firm commitments to sustained investment would tend to support semiconductor and AI hardware names further up the supply chain. UBS’s warning about company-specific volatility suggests results may produce sharper winners and losers than the broad AI trade has seen. Meta’s report sets the early tone, as an advertising-led business funding heavy AI investment.

Earlier:

  • Stock earnings pick of the week: Meta faces a $145 billion question after the tech rout
  • What is earnings season and why the first companies to report are important to watch

UBS says the AI trade has moved past the adoption story: this earnings season, big tech has to show the spending is turning into revenue, profit and returns.

Summary:

  • Meta’s results after the US close on Wednesday open the reporting season for mega-cap tech
  • UBS says rising rates and higher financing costs put AI monetisation and capex returns under closer scrutiny
  • Its three tests: health of core businesses, AI monetisation beyond adoption, and tangible returns on infrastructure spending
  • UBS expects a strong third quarter fundamentally but warns elevated expectations may cause company-specific volatility
  • It remains constructive on the structural AI opportunity, favouring hyperscalers and high-quality semiconductor and hardware beneficiaries

Big US technology companies need to show this earnings season that artificial intelligence can generate returns large enough to justify heavy capital spending, according to UBS, which has set out three tests that it says could shape the AI trade into 2027.

Meta Platforms opens mega-cap tech reporting when it releases third-quarter results after the US close on Wednesday, with its conference call at 4.30pm ET (20:30 GMT). UBS said rising interest rates and higher financing costs mean investors are looking harder at whether AI can drive meaningful revenue while capital spending weighs on free cash flow. The bank did not take a view on any single company.

The first test is the health of core businesses. UBS said the largest tech groups enter the season with strong positions in advertising, software, devices and digital commerce, and that continued demand in those areas helps fund AI investment while cushioning earnings. The question is whether recent growth can hold up as year-on-year comparisons get tougher and economic risks persist.

The second is monetisation. Rising use of AI products is encouraging, UBS said, but investors increasingly want evidence that usage translates into revenue and profit, whether through subscriptions, consumption-based pricing, advertising, transactions or greater cloud utilisation. Clarity on pricing and customer willingness to pay would strengthen the case that AI is becoming a revenue driver rather than mainly an investment programme.

The third is returns on spending. Even if AI revenue grows, the scale of infrastructure investment has implications for margins and cash flow. UBS said investors will focus on capacity utilisation, pricing power, capital requirements and returns on AI investment, with management commentary on the future pace of capex likely to shape expectations for 2027 and beyond.

Overall, UBS expects a strong quarter from a fundamental perspective but cautioned that elevated expectations could produce company-specific volatility. It remains constructive on the long-term AI opportunity, seeing value in hyperscalers and high-quality semiconductor and hardware companies, while suggesting investors with concentrated tech holdings consider rebalancing across sectors and regions during periods of strength.

With Meta first up and other mega-cap names following in the coming weeks, capex guidance is likely to matter as much as the quarterly numbers themselves.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Super Micro shares jump 14% as preliminary revenue tops forecast by about $4 billion
item.description:
The update gives the AI hardware trade a fresh demand signal, and the after-hours moves in Dell and HPE show investors treating it as a read-through for the wider server group rather than a company-specific win. That matters given both stocks fell heavily last week, so the rebound may test whether that selling was overdone. The margin beat could carry more weight than the revenue figure, as it eases a long-running concern that Super Micro has had to trade profitability for volume. With limited detail until 3 November, the open question is customer concentration: how much of the surge comes from the large cloud providers versus newer AI-focused buyers, whose spending may be less durable.

Super Micro did not just sell far more AI servers than expected, it kept more of the money from each one, and that combination briefly lifted the whole server sector.

Summary:

  • Super Micro released a surprise preliminary update for the September quarter, ahead of full results on 3 November
  • Revenue is now expected at $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, against prior guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion and analyst expectations of about $15 billion
  • The midpoint implies revenue growth of nearly 280% from a year earlier
  • Gross margin is estimated at 12% to 12.5%, above the previous 10.4% to 10.8% outlook
  • Super Micro shares rose 14% in extended trading; Dell gained 6% and HPE 5%
  • The split of sales between major cloud companies and newer AI cloud providers is not yet known

Super Micro Computer shares jumped 14% in extended trading on Tuesday after the AI server maker released a surprise preliminary update showing September-quarter revenue and profitability well ahead of its own guidance and Wall Street expectations.

The company now expects revenue of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion for the quarter, compared with its earlier forecast of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. Analysts tracked by FactSet had expected about $15 billion. The midpoint of the new range points to growth of nearly 280% from the same quarter a year earlier, a pace that reflects heavy spending on AI computing infrastructure.

Profitability, a recurring concern for Super Micro investors, also improved. The company estimates gross margin of 12% to 12.5% for the quarter, above its previous outlook of 10.4% to 10.8%. Gross margin measures how much revenue a company keeps after covering the direct costs of making its products. Super Micro’s margins remain thin by technology hardware standards, but the improvement suggests it is gaining some pricing power in a market where rival Dell Technologies has historically commanded a premium on AI servers.

Analysts described the update as a positive sign for AI compute demand, and one noted that the combination of stronger sales and better margins bodes well for other server makers. Dell shares rose 6% after hours and Hewlett Packard Enterprise gained 5%, recovering some ground after heavy losses last week.

The release came on a busy day for technology investors, landing alongside SpaceX’s quarterly results, which also showed strong AI-related revenue.

Super Micro’s update was brief, covering only a handful of figures with little commentary. One key unknown, analysts said, is how much of the quarter’s business came from the major cloud providers compared with newer AI-focused cloud companies such as CoreWeave and SpaceX. That mix will shape how investors judge the durability of the growth.

A fuller picture is due when Super Micro reports official results on 3 November, when investors will look for guidance on whether the current quarter can sustain the pace. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs says 6% nominal growth, not 5% yields, is what matters for small caps
item.description:
The note offers a framework for holding small caps even if Treasury yields stay elevated, which could support rotation flows toward the segment as long as growth data hold up. The flip side is that the thesis is explicitly tied to nominal growth, so small caps may become more sensitive to economic data surprises than to moves in yields, with a softer PMI or GDP print a bigger threat than a rate rise. Goldman’s view that inflation pressure is largely energy-driven also links the outlook to oil: a further spike in crude would test the argument that broader inflation is moderating. The emphasis on dispersion suggests index-level small-cap exposure may lag a more selective approach.

-

Earlier:

  • Netflix tops Q3 profit forecast but trims two full-year targets as Q4 guide disappoints
  • SpaceX beats Q3 forecasts across all three segments as AI revenue tops $7.5 billion

-

Goldman Sachs argues small-cap investors are watching the wrong number: the growth backdrop, not the 10-year yield, is what decides whether the asset class works.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says the key question for small caps is whether nominal growth stays healthy, not whether the 10-year yield is above 5%
  • Small caps have historically done best when nominal GDP is above 5% and accelerating; it is currently running near 6%, with real GDP around 2.3%
  • The bank notes small caps have generally delivered positive returns during periods of sharply rising rates
  • It expects U.S. growth of about 2.3%, unemployment near 4% and contained recession risk, with PMIs at their highest in more than five years
  • Inflation looks narrower than headline figures suggest, with much of the pressure energy-related
  • Valuations look attractive versus large caps and history, and a higher cost of capital should favour active stock selection

Goldman Sachs says investors weighing small-cap stocks should focus less on the level of interest rates and more on the strength of nominal economic growth, arguing in a new note that the growth backdrop currently favours the asset class.

The bank said the central question is not whether the 10-year Treasury yield sits above 5%, but whether nominal growth remains healthy. Small caps have historically performed best when nominal GDP, which combines real growth and inflation, is above 5% and accelerating, according to Goldman Sachs. Nominal GDP is currently running near 6% year on year, with real GDP at around 2.3%.

Goldman Sachs said higher rates alone have not historically been a reason to avoid small caps, noting the group has generally posted positive returns during periods of sharply rising rates.

The bank’s macro outlook supports that view. It expects U.S. growth of about 2.3%, unemployment near 4% and relatively contained recession risk, while purchasing managers’ indices have reached their highest levels in more than five years. Goldman Sachs also said inflation looks narrower than headline figures suggest, with much of the pressure coming from energy and broader measures continuing to moderate.

On fundamentals, the bank said earnings strength among smaller companies appears to be broadening rather than concentrating in a handful of names. It described valuations as attractive relative to both large caps and historical levels, offering what it sees as a compelling entry point alongside improving fundamentals.

Goldman Sachs added that a rising cost of capital raises the bar for companies, rewarding profitability, durable earnings and strong returns on capital while penalising weaker businesses. That widening gap between winners and losers, it said, may create a more favourable environment for stock picking and active management.

The argument rests on growth holding up. If nominal GDP slows meaningfully, or energy-driven inflation broadens into wider price pressure that forces rates higher still, the conditions Goldman Sachs identifies as supportive for small caps would weaken. For now, the bank sees the growth backdrop doing more of the work than the rate debate suggests. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More from RBA’s (hawkish) Hauser: Q3 trimmed mean set to run hotter than expected
item.description:
Flagging a higher-than-expected trimmed mean a week before the official CPI release is an unusually direct steer, and it shifts the risk balance for 28 October toward an upside surprise. Combined with his view that capacity pressures are tighter than the RBA assumed, the remarks are likely to reinforce hike pricing for 3 November, which would tend to support the Australian dollar and lift short-end Australian yields. His comment on supply shocks matters for the oil channel: it suggests the RBA is less inclined to look through energy-driven price rises while expectations are at risk, making crude a more direct input into Australian rate pricing. Softer labour data gives the doves a counterweight, but Hauser’s framing suggests it is not enough on its own to keep the Board on hold.

---

RBA 2026 dates, next meeting in just a couple of weeks time:

-

Hauser has all but previewed a hot underlying inflation print, and with capacity tighter than assumed and supply shocks no longer something to look through, a softer jobs market looks like a footnote rather than a reprieve.

Summary:

  • Hauser said the quarterly trimmed mean inflation measure looks like it will be higher than the RBA expected
  • He said capacity pressures in the economy are more elevated than anticipated
  • The RBA has to respond to supply shocks to keep inflation expectations anchored, he said
  • Policy cannot target current inflation, but that does not mean current inflation is unimportant
  • September labour data was a little weaker than expected; unemployment remains quite low but the labour market is easing
  • September-quarter CPI is due on 28 October, ahead of the RBA’s 3 November decision

More from Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser, who signalled that underlying inflation for the September quarter is likely to come in above the central bank’s expectations, adding to his earlier comments that the inflation outlook looks worse than forecast.

Speaking at Citi’s Australia and New Zealand Investment Conference in Sydney, Hauser said the quarterly trimmed mean appeared set to be higher than the RBA had expected. The trimmed mean strips out the largest price rises and falls each quarter to give a clearer read on underlying inflation, and it is the measure the RBA watches most closely. His remark comes a week before the Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes September-quarter inflation data on 28 October.

Hauser also said capacity pressures in the economy were more elevated than the RBA had anticipated, suggesting demand is still running further ahead of supply than policymakers assumed.

On supply shocks, Hauser said the RBA has to respond to them in order to keep inflation expectations anchored. Central banks often look through supply-driven price rises on the basis that they fade over time, but his comments suggest the RBA sees less room to do so after a long period of high inflation. The RBA has previously pointed to the Middle East conflict and its effect on oil prices as a supply-side pressure.

He added that monetary policy cannot target current inflation, since it works with a lag, but stressed that this does not mean current inflation is irrelevant, as persistent price rises can feed into expectations.

The labour market offered a partial offset. Hauser said September’s employment report was clearly a little weaker than expected and that while unemployment remains quite low, conditions are easing.

The RBA lifted its cash rate to 4.60% on 29 September. The Board meets on 2 and 3 November, with the decision due at 2.30pm Sydney time on 3 November (03:30 GMT, 22:30 ET on 2 November), alongside updated staff forecasts. A trimmed mean result above expectations next week would likely leave a further rate rise firmly on the table.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike
item.description:
The poll firms up December as the likely window for the BOJ’s next move, which should limit yen sensitivity to the 30 October meeting but raises the stakes around the December decision. The bigger currency risk may be the vote itself: with the yen only modestly above its 2026 low, a repeat of September’s dissent from government-nominated board members could be read as political resistance to tightening and trigger fresh selling. Rising energy and import costs tied to the Middle East war keep oil a direct input into Japan’s inflation outlook, so a further jump in crude would likely harden the case for hikes. For JGBs, the shift toward a 2% or higher terminal rate, combined with fiscal concerns, points to continued pressure on yields.

-

Economists now broadly expect the BOJ to keep raising rates every quarter, with the main risk to the yen coming not from the timing of the next move but from who votes against it.

Summary:

  • 69% of economists (54 of 78) in an October 13 to 19 Reuters poll expect the BOJ to lift its policy rate to 1.50% this quarter, up from 36% in September
  • Of those naming a month, about 80% picked December; only 2% chose the meeting ending 30 October
  • 60% expect the rate to reach 1.75% by end-June 2027; 51% now see a terminal rate of 2.00% or higher, up from 40% in September
  • Nearly three-quarters said further dissent at the next hike could weigh on the yen, which is only about 4% above its 2026 low near 164 per dollar
  • Nearly two-thirds expect the government to keep new bond issuance below 40 trillion yen for fiscal 2027

The Bank of Japan is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate to 1.50% in December, according to a Reuters poll of economists, extending a pattern of quarterly increases after hikes in June and September.

Of 78 economists surveyed between 13 and 19 October, 54, or nearly 70%, expected a move to 1.50% this quarter, almost double the share in the September poll. About 80% of those naming a month chose December, while just 2% expected action at the BOJ’s two-day meeting ending on 30 October.

Higher energy and import costs, made worse by a weak yen and the war in the Middle East, are adding to inflation pressure, the poll found. A period of relative stability in the yen, which faced heavy selling for much of the year and prompted intervention from both Japanese authorities and the US Treasury, also supports the case for a December move. Board member Junko Koeda said last week the BOJ should not become overly cautious about raising rates, now at their highest in 31 years, given significant upside risks to inflation.

Not every economist sees the need for speed. Some argued the economy is not overheating enough to justify back-to-back hikes and that prices remain within the BOJ’s expected range. Sources have told Reuters that many BOJ officials want more data on how earlier increases have affected financial conditions.

Expectations for the peak rate have shifted higher. Sixty per cent of respondents saw the policy rate at 1.75% by the end of June next year, while the share expecting it to reach 2.00% or more rose to 51% from 40% in September.

Politics remains a risk for the yen. In September, two board members nominated by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who favour looser fiscal policy, voted against raising rates to 1.25%. Nearly three-quarters of economists said further dissent at the next hike could weigh on the yen, which sits only about 4% above its 2026 low near 164 per dollar.

On fiscal policy, nearly two-thirds of respondents expected the government to keep new bond issuance below 40 trillion yen, about $250 billion, for fiscal 2027, after Takaichi said she aims to hold issuance around that level.

With the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank also expected to raise rates in December, according to separate Reuters polls, the BOJ’s next decision will be judged as much on the vote split as on the move itself.

A personal note: I write article after article on the Bank of Japan outlook and every shift in economists’ views, but if I had simply written “a quarterly pace of rate rises” and left it at that, I reckon I’d have been 99% correct.

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA’s Hauser says inflation outlook worse than forecast ahead of 3 November decision
item.description:
Hauser’s remarks lean hawkish, very IMO, and are likely to keep a further rate rise in play for 3 November, which would tend to support the Australian dollar and push short-dated Australian yields higher if markets add to hike pricing. His acknowledgment of slowing labour and housing data offers the doves something to work with, but his emphasis on inflation expectations suggests the bar for holding is rising. The September-quarter CPI on 28 October now looks decisive: an upside surprise would strengthen the case for a fifth hike this year. Energy prices remain a wildcard, with the RBA having previously cited the Middle East conflict and its effect on oil as a complication layered on top of domestic demand pressures.

---

Hauser stopped short of pre-announcing a hike, but an inflation outlook running worse than forecast and a warning on expectations leave November firmly live.

Earlier:

  • RBA’s Kent says neutral rate is rising, questions if policy is restrictive enough

Summary:

  • RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook looks worse than forecast, a bit above expectations
  • He said inflation has been high for a very long time and the RBA cannot allow inflation expectations to move away from target
  • Businesses are reporting cost pressures as their number one problem
  • He acknowledged some slowing in labour market and housing data and said monetary policy is working
  • Staff forecasts are still being finalised and he does not know for sure what the Board will decide
  • The cash rate is 4.60% after a hike on 29 September; the next decision is due on 3 November, with Q3 CPI out on 28 October

Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook looks worse than the central bank had forecast, in comments that lean hawkish less than two weeks before the RBA’s next policy decision on 3 November.

Speaking at a fireside chat at Citi’s Australia and New Zealand Investment Conference in Sydney on Wednesday morning, Hauser said the outlook for inflation was running a little above expectations. He stressed that inflation had been high for a very long time and that the RBA could not allow inflation expectations to drift away from its target, a signal that policymakers see the risk of price pressures becoming entrenched as a growing concern.

Hauser said businesses were reporting cost pressures as their number one problem. He acknowledged some slowing in labour market and housing data and said monetary policy was working, but added that the inflation outlook had nonetheless deteriorated.

He was careful not to pre-empt the Board. Hauser said staff were still finalising their forecasts and that he did not know for certain what the Board would decide. The November meeting comes with a fresh set of RBA economic projections, which will show how far the inflation outlook has shifted.

The RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60% on 29 September, a unanimous decision and the fourth increase of 2026. Hauser has been among the RBA’s most consistent voices on inflation this year, previously describing it as the bank’s one big problem and pointing to the Middle East conflict, an artificial intelligence-driven global boom and weak supply capacity as drivers.

The next major test arrives on 28 October with the release of September-quarter inflation data, the last key input before the Board meets on 2 and 3 November. The decision is due at 2.30pm Sydney time on 3 November (03:30 GMT, 22:30 ET on 2 November). With Hauser signalling that the outlook has worsened and that expectations must stay anchored, a stronger-than-expected CPI print would likely strengthen the case for a fifth rate rise this year.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: JPMorgan sees Bitcoin returning 10% a year: why volatility makes that hard to collect
item.description:
JPMorgan expects Bitcoin to return 10% a year. Here is why that number is harder to hold than it looks

J.P. Morgan Asset Management has put a long-term return forecast on Bitcoin for the first time. Its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, the 31st edition of the firm’s annual 10 to 15 year outlook, project a compound return of about 10% a year, according to reports on the document. That is higher than the firm’s 7.5% forecast for US large-cap stocks. JPMorgan has not added Bitcoin to its main portfolio models, though, and the reason it gives is the most useful lesson in the report.

What JPMorgan actually said

The firm says that for the first time it has put a range on Bitcoin returns. It has not included Bitcoin in its main covariance matrices, the models it uses to estimate how assets move together when building portfolios. Instead, it built a separate, smaller set comparing Bitcoin with a subset of public-market assets.

JPMorgan said Bitcoin’s volatility and unstable correlations with other assets remain an obstacle to wider portfolio inclusion. Reports on the document put its volatility assumption at about 55% a year, against roughly 18% for US large-cap stocks. The analysts said they could revisit the approach if volatility falls and correlations settle, particularly as regulation, liquidity and price discovery improve.

So this is a forecast, not an allocation. JPMorgan is telling clients what it expects Bitcoin might return, not recommending they own it.

The lesson: average returns and compound returns are not the same

Long-term forecasts like this one are usually quoted as compound returns, the rate at which money actually grows over time. That is different from the simple average of yearly returns, and the gap between the two widens as volatility rises.

A simple example shows why. Imagine two investments, each with an average return of 10% a year over two years. The first gains 10% in year one and 10% in year two. A $100 stake grows to $121. The second gains 60% in year one and then loses 40% in year two. The average is still 10%, but the $100 becomes $160 and then $96. The investor has lost money.

This effect is often called volatility drag. Large losses do more damage than equally large gains repair, because a fall applies to a bigger or smaller base than the rise before it. A common rule of thumb is that the compound return sits below the average return by roughly half the variance, the square of volatility.

For an asset with 18% volatility, that drag is modest, about 1.6 percentage points. At 55% volatility, the same rule of thumb suggests a gap of roughly 15 percentage points. In other words, for Bitcoin to compound at 10% a year at that level of volatility, its average yearly return would need to be far higher. Treat that as an illustration of the mechanism rather than JPMorgan’s own arithmetic.

Why this matters for investors

The headline comparison, 10% for Bitcoin against 7.5% for US stocks, compares compound returns but not the ride. An investor who sells after a deep drawdown may never collect the long-term compound figure at all. Position size matters for the same reason. A small allocation to a highly volatile asset can be held through large swings; a large one is far harder to sit through.

This is also why JPMorgan’s correlation caveat matters. Portfolio models rely on assets behaving in reasonably predictable ways relative to each other. If Bitcoin sometimes trades like a technology stock and sometimes on its own, it is hard to say how much it diversifies a portfolio, and the firm says that instability impairs a strategic allocation.

There is a countercase. Bitwise chief investment officer Matt Hougan welcomed the forecast but argued that a 55% volatility assumption is too high, pointing to Bitcoin’s falling volatility over the past 15 years. If he is right, the drag would be smaller and the case for an allocation stronger.

What to watch next

  • Bitcoin’s realized volatility. A sustained fall would be the clearest sign that JPMorgan’s main obstacle is easing.
  • Correlation behavior. Watch whether Bitcoin keeps moving with the Nasdaq during risk-off periods or starts to trade more independently.
  • Next year’s LTCMA. If JPMorgan moves Bitcoin into its main covariance matrices, that would be the shift from forecasting to modeling, and a far stronger signal than the 10% figure.

The practical takeaway: a high expected return does not tell you whether you can hold an asset long enough to earn it. Volatility decides that, and for now JPMorgan thinks Bitcoin’s volatility is still too high.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic IPO draft shows nearly 15-fold revenue jump and $600 billion in compute deals
item.description:
The commitments disclosed in the filing amount to multi-year revenue visibility for Anthropic’s infrastructure suppliers, with Google, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Broadcom each tied to contracts running into the tens or hundreds of billions of dollars, much of it noncancelable. That may support the case that AI infrastructure demand is contracted rather than speculative, though it also concentrates counterparty risk on a single loss-making buyer. For prospective IPO investors, the debate is likely to centre on whether revenue growth can keep outrunning compute costs, and on customer concentration, with two clients contributing around a fifth of first-half sales. A valuation of up to $2 trillion would leave little room for a slowdown on either front.

Anthropic’s draft prospectus shows a company growing faster than its costs, but committed to an infrastructure bill so large that its suppliers, customers and regulators all become part of the investment case.

Summary:

  • First-half 2026 revenue of about $16.3 billion, up from about $1.1 billion a year earlier, according to a draft prospectus viewed by the Wall Street Journal (gated)
  • Net loss of about $81 billion for the half, of which roughly $72 billion came from accounting charges tied to convertible notes and other financing instruments; the prior-year half-year loss was about $13 billion
  • Compute and infrastructure spending of nearly $9 billion in the half, more than in all of 2025
  • Infrastructure commitments exceed $600 billion, with further deals under negotiation that could add up to $150 billion
  • Around a fifth of first-half revenue came from two customers
  • Risk factors include AI safety and liability, possible uninsurable catastrophic incidents, constrained compute access and organised opposition to data centres

Anthropic grew revenue nearly fifteenfold in the first half of 2026 while committing to more than $600 billion in future computing infrastructure, according to a draft initial public offering prospectus reviewed by the Wall Street Journal. The company declined to comment on the report.

The artificial intelligence developer generated about $16.3 billion in revenue in the six months to 30 June, compared with about $1.1 billion a year earlier, the Journal reported. That is already well above the roughly $4.6 billion it brought in during all of 2025. Spending on computing capacity and infrastructure rose to nearly $9 billion in the half, from about $2.3 billion a year earlier, and exceeded the company’s full-year 2025 outlay of around $7.3 billion.

The headline loss is far larger. Anthropic recorded a net loss of about $81 billion for the half, against roughly $13 billion a year earlier and about $42 billion for the whole of 2025. Around $72 billion of that reflected accounting charges linked to changes in the value of convertible notes and other instruments used to raise funding, rather than operating costs.

The scale of Anthropic’s infrastructure commitments is the filing’s most striking feature. According to the Journal, the company owes around $450 billion under cloud agreements over the next seven to 10 years, most of which cannot be cancelled. That includes about $111 billion with Google, $110 billion with Amazon Web Services and $31 billion with Microsoft, plus up to $86 billion for Nvidia chip capacity from Nscale and Lambda. A separate obligation of more than $160 billion to lease Google chips through Broadcom lifts the total above $600 billion, and deals still under negotiation could add up to $150 billion more.

Even so, the company said its major cloud partners had not provided as much capacity as it sought, and that those partners increasingly view it as a competitor. Anthropic is supplementing that capacity with leased data centres and third-party operators, some of which it said have short track records.

Revenue is also concentrated. Two customers accounted for about a fifth of first-half sales, and the company expects a large share of revenue to keep coming from a small group of clients.

Risk factors make up roughly a third of the document, the Journal reported. They include the possibility of misaligned AI models causing harm, liability for damages such as data theft, and incidents severe enough that insurance may not cover them. Anthropic also cited increasingly coordinated political opposition to data centre construction, noting that its public profile could draw attention to projects linked to it.

The filing comes as Anthropic prepares for a listing that could value it at up to $2 trillion, putting its growth rate, cost base and customer mix under far closer public scrutiny than before.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Boeing wins FAA approval for 737 MAX 10, unlocking nearly 1,500 orders after 7-year wait
item.description:
Certification removes one of the largest overhangs on Boeing’s stock, given how sharply shares reacted to the last delay, falling nearly 7% in late September when a software glitch put approval on hold. The bigger financial prize is cash flow: Boeing has been carrying dozens of completed but undelivered MAX 7 and MAX 10 jets, and converting that inventory into deliveries should support cash generation over the next year or more. Attention now shifts to Boeing’s third-quarter results on 27 October, where investors will look for a delivery timeline and any update to cash flow guidance. For Airbus, the approval ends a long period in which the A321neo faced no direct rival at the top of the single-aisle market.

---

Seven years late and one software scare later, Boeing finally has its answer to the A321neo cleared to fly, and with it a large backlog it can at last start turning into cash.

Summary:

  • The FAA granted final certification to the 737 MAX 10 on Tuesday, the largest variant of Boeing’s best-selling jet family
  • The approval clears the way for deliveries against nearly 1,500 orders, about 30% of the 737 backlog
  • United Airlines is the largest customer with 167 firm orders; Alaska Airlines holds 105, with Ryanair, Delta and American also major buyers
  • The first MAX 10 rolled out in November 2019 and was originally due to enter service in 2020
  • Delays stemmed from the 2019 to 2020 MAX grounding, tighter FAA oversight, an engine anti-ice flaw and, most recently, a software issue disclosed in September
  • The aircraft seats 185 to 230 passengers with a range of about 3,100 nautical miles

The US Federal Aviation Administration has certified Boeing’s 737 MAX 10, clearing the largest model in the planemaker’s best-selling jet family for customer deliveries after a delay of almost seven years. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was scheduled to mark the approval at Boeing’s factory in Everett, Washington, on Tuesday.

The decision unlocks close to 1,500 orders, roughly 30% of Boeing’s total 737 backlog. United Airlines is the largest customer, with 167 firm orders, followed by Alaska Airlines with 105. Ryanair, Delta Air Lines and American Airlines are also significant buyers. The MAX 10 seats between 185 and 230 passengers and flies about 3,100 nautical miles, positioning it against the Airbus A321neo at the top end of the single-aisle market.

The first MAX 10 rolled off the line in November 2019, with service entry originally planned for 2020. The programme was then caught up in the worldwide MAX grounding that followed two fatal crashes, tighter certification standards and closer FAA scrutiny after a door panel blew out of a 737 MAX 9 in flight in January 2024. A flaw in the engine anti-ice system, identified in 2023, added further delay because running the system continuously could overheat the engine inlet.

The final stretch was not smooth either. In late September, Boeing disclosed a software issue that could prevent pilots from using automated flight guidance in a specific landing scenario, and the FAA said it would hold off on approval until the problem was resolved, according to Reuters. Boeing shares fell close to 7% that day. The regulator later allowed certification to proceed while Boeing works on a permanent software update. Flight testing had already been completed in July, after nearly 1,000 flights and more than 2,060 hours in the air.

The approval follows certification of the smaller MAX 7 in August. Boeing said in its most recent quarterly filing that it held about 40 completed MAX 7 and MAX 10 aircraft in inventory at the end of June, and chief executive Kelly Ortberg has said the company expects to work through stored jets of both models over roughly 18 months.

Production capacity is also building. Boeing opened a new 737 line in Everett in July to supplement output in Renton, and is moving its 737 production rate from 42 to 47 aircraft a month, with further increases planned. The new Everett line must be production-certified by the FAA before it can deliver aircraft.

Analysts have long seen MAX 10 deliveries as critical to restoring Boeing’s revenue and cash flow. The company reports third-quarter results on 27 October, when investors will be watching for a firm delivery schedule and any change to its cash flow outlook. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Swiss regulator FINMA approves first retail Bitcoin ETF, waives diversification rules
item.description:
Switzerland approves its first Bitcoin ETF for retail investors: what has actually changed

Switzerland’s financial regulator, FINMA, has approved the country’s first exchange-traded fund that holds Bitcoin directly and is open to ordinary investors. The approval, announced on Tuesday 20 October, changes how Swiss retail investors can own Bitcoin, but it does not yet put any new money into the market. FINMA did not name the fund or its issuer, and no launch date has been given.

What FINMA approved

The product is an investment fund under Swiss law, classified as an “other fund for alternative investments” with special risk. That distinction is the real news. Swiss investors have been able to buy Bitcoin exchange-traded products for some time, but those are structured products, effectively debt instruments issued by a provider. The new ETF sits under Swiss fund law instead, with its own requirements on custody, risk management and investor disclosure.

FINMA said it had seen growing interest in crypto investments, particularly Bitcoin, and that other fund providers have already submitted or announced applications for Bitcoin ETFs.

Why Bitcoin got an exception

Funds sold to the public are normally required to spread their money across many holdings. A fund holding a single asset breaks that rule by design, so FINMA granted an exemption from the diversification requirements. Its reasoning was that Bitcoin has a long trading history and a particularly high trading volume compared with other cryptocurrencies.

In plain terms, the regulator is treating Bitcoin’s depth and track record as the condition that makes concentration in one asset acceptable for a retail fund. On my reading, that is a Bitcoin-specific judgment rather than a general green light for single-coin funds.

The contrast with FINMA’s earlier crypto approval is useful. In 2021 it authorized a fund that invested mainly in a basket of cryptocurrencies, and that product was restricted to qualified investors. This is the first time Swiss retail investors get a regulated fund holding Bitcoin alone.

The safeguards attached

FINMA paired the approval with several conditions. Supervised institutions must reduce operational and custody risks in line with supervisory guidance the regulator published in January 2026. Firms selling the fund must follow the conduct rules of the Swiss Financial Services Act at the point of sale, including clear warnings about volatility and the risk of losses, and checks on whether the product is appropriate or suitable for the buyer. The fund documents must also set out the risks clearly.

FINMA argued that these rules give investors more protection than buying cryptocurrency directly. It also stressed that Bitcoin remains a high-risk investment even inside an approved ETF, that invested capital can lose a substantial part of its value, and that investors should keep this in mind when deciding how much to put in.

What this does not mean

An approval is not a launch, and a launch is not demand. Until the fund is named, listed and trading, there are no flows to measure. Even then, early Swiss flows should not be read as evidence of broad institutional buying without data to support it.

What to watch next

  • The issuer and launch date. These will show how quickly the approval turns into a product investors can actually buy.
  • Further approvals. FINMA has confirmed other applications are in the pipeline. Several launches would make this a competition story on fees and custody arrangements.
  • Whether the exemption travels. FINMA’s reasoning rests on trading history and volume. Any future single-asset fund for another cryptocurrency, such as Ether, would need to clear the same bar.
  • Early flows once trading starts. Modest initial flows would not change the broader Bitcoin picture. The more durable significance is structural: a fund-law route into Bitcoin for Swiss retail investors.

What could change this reading: a delayed launch or a narrowly drawn exemption would make the approval look more like a one-off. A quick succession of launches from several providers would make it a template for regulated retail access in Europe. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Wednesday, October 21, 2026: ECB Lane speaking
item.description:
The data is not expected to be too impactful, but we do hear from Lane later. 

'

ECB’s Lane in Shanghai: three officials set the scene for a 29 October decision

ECB chief economist Philip Lane joins a panel on the international monetary system beyond the dollar in Shanghai today at 04:15 GMT (00:15 ET). It is a closed-door luncheon on a structural theme, so a direct policy steer is unlikely, although the ECB says it will publish the text.

The policy backdrop is well established. The ECB raised its deposit rate by a quarter point in June and again in September, taking it to 2.50%. Markets and most economists expect a hold on 29 October and a hike in December.

Lane’s most recent policy remarks came in a 5 October speech, where he described the recent surge in energy prices as a second wave of the energy supply shock, posing upside risks to inflation but downside risks to growth. He noted September inflation reached 3.8%, with energy inflation at about 19% compared with around 2% for non-energy prices, a split that supports patience on rates.

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel, among the Governing Council’s more hawkish members, has sounded less urgent than his reputation suggests. He said inflation risks remain tilted to the upside and higher energy prices could keep inflation elevated for longer, but that longer-term expectations remain broadly anchored around 2%. Crucially, he pointed to an absence of inflation feeding through to price and wage setting, which leaves room to wait in October.

President Christine Lagarde has pushed in the same direction. She said rates do not move in lockstep with energy prices, while acknowledging energy is a significant variable. Speaking last week, she said there were no second-round effects yet, but that the ECB cannot wait until they are in full view.

The decision is due at 13:15 GMT (09:15 ET) on 29 October. October is a meeting without new staff projections, which next arrive with the December meeting ending on 17 December. That makes December the more natural window for any further hike, with energy prices and wage data the key inputs in between.

item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 20 Oct: USD falls as deal headlines swing oil; Dow and small caps outperform
item.description:
• Netflix tops Q3 profit forecast but trims two full-year targets as Q4 guide disappoints
  • Trump: Ukraine has to want to settle this war, if not it's going to be a very bad thing
  • Finland President Stubb offers some optimism for Russia-Ukraine peace
  • BOE's Greene keeps banging the hawkish drum, and she’s not alone anymore
  • European stocks close mostly lower as Middle East headlines drive market swings
  • Iran and US talks continue. Reports that a deal is close are wrong
  • Treasury Sec. Bessent says we are on the "other side of the energy shock". The price action needs to confirm that claim.
  • US September pending home sales -7.3% vs -0.5% expected
  • Bitcoin Technicals: Sellers regain control, but the range floor remains the next test
  • Iran agreed to secret nuclear site visits in shift towards compromise, report says
  • US September housing starts 1.221M vs 1.305M
  • Morning Kickstart: Dollar mixed as oil tops $100 and European stocks retreat
  • investingLive European news wrap: Rising oil prices keep weighing on risk sentiment

Markets spent Tuesday responding to competing messages. Reports of progress toward a US–Iran agreement sent oil and Treasury yields lower and weighed on the dollar. A subsequent report that negotiations were continuing but a deal was not close took some of the optimism out of that move. Meanwhile, disappointing US housing data provided a reminder that elevated borrowing costs are taking a toll.

The result was a session that offered relief without resolving the bigger questions. The dollar was lower against all the major currencies. The Dow and Russell 2000 posted solid gains, but the Nasdaq struggled to hold positive territory. Long-term Treasury yields fell, while shorter-term yields edged higher. There was buying, but the markets were hardly delivering an all-clear signal.

Dollar lower, with sterling leading

The dollar’s largest decline came against the British pound. GBPUSD rose 0.59% to 1.3380 after trading as high as 1.3409. The Canadian dollar also advanced, with USDCAD falling 0.35% to 1.4061. AUDUSD and NZDUSD each gained 0.32%, reaching 0.7000 and 0.5680, respectively.

Elsewhere, EURUSD rose 0.22% to 1.1235, USDCHF fell 0.23% to 0.8246, and USDJPY declined 0.16% to 158.23. The dollar’s smallest loss was against the yen.

The breadth of the decline matters. This was more than a move in one currency pair. Lower long-term US yields and the possibility of reduced geopolitical tensions helped undermine the dollar’s support. However, the retreat from the day’s extremes showed how quickly that trade could lose momentum when the headlines became less encouraging.

Treasury curve flattens as the long end rallies

The Treasury market delivered a more nuanced message than simply “yields fell.” In the supplied late-session snapshot, the 2-year yield was 4.7846%, up 2.36 basis points, and the 5-year was 4.9345%, up 0.55 basis point. Further out, the 10-year yield fell 2.13 basis points to 5.1147%, while the 30-year declined 4.99 basis points to 5.4231%.

That combination flattened the yield curve. Longer-term borrowing costs eased, but the short end offered little evidence of a broad repricing toward easier Fed policy.

For the economy, lower long-term yields would be welcome if sustained. Housing needs some relief. But one session of falling yields does not erase the pressure from financing costs that remain elevated.

Dow and small caps outperform; Nasdaq stalls

The supplied late-session stock snapshot showed:

  • Dow industrial average: 52,501.24, up 530.05 points or 1.02%.

  • S&P 500: 7,712.69, up 21.96 points or 0.29%.

  • Nasdaq Composite: 26,424.82, down 6.07 points or 0.02%.

  • Russell 2000: 2,776.5767, up 48.2787 points or 1.77%.

  • Nasdaq 100: 29,490.28, down 39.06 points or 0.13%.

The divergence was the story. Small caps and the Dow attracted buyers, while the technology-heavy indices lagged. The S&P’s modest advance sat between those two outcomes.

Lower long-term yields can help smaller companies by easing financing concerns, but the Nasdaq’s inability to participate showed that cheaper yields alone were not enough to produce a broad technology rally. Buyers were willing to take on some risk. They remained selective about where they put it.

European equities were mostly lower, with Spain bucking the softer trend, according to InvestingLive’s European close report. The regional contrast reinforced the uneven nature of the day’s recovery.

After-hours earnings: SpaceX rises; Netflix guidance disappoints

SpaceX and Netflix delivered earnings beats after the close, but the initial share-price reactions went in opposite directions. SpaceX shares were trading up 2.15% at $150.90, while Netflix fell 3.33% to $66.40 as investors focused on disappointing guidance.

SpaceX reported quarterly earnings of $0.35 per share versus $0.17 expected, with revenue of $14.6 billion topping the $12.98 billion estimate. Adjusted EBITDA also comfortably exceeded expectations at approximately $8.8 billion versus $6.72 billion forecast. Operating income improved to $2.79 billion from a loss a year earlier, pointing to stronger profitability. However, capital spending climbed to $19.59 billion from $6.88 billion. That leaves investors balancing the stronger results against the substantial cost of expansion.

For Netflix, the backward-looking numbers were better than expected. Earnings of $0.87 per share beat the $0.82 estimate, while revenue of $14.6 billion exceeded expectations of $12.9 billion. Free cash flow, however, missed forecasts at $2.88 billion versus $3.22 billion expected.

The bigger disappointment came from the outlook. Netflix projected fourth-quarter earnings of $0.67 per share versus $0.73 expected and revenue of $13.4 billion versus $13.5 billion forecast. Its projected operating margin of 26% also fell short of the 27.6% estimate. Full-year free-cash-flow guidance was approximately $12 billion, down from around $12.5 billion previously.

The reaction is a reminder that an earnings beat does not guarantee a higher share price. Investors also price what comes next, and Netflix’s guidance gave sellers a reason to lean on the shares. At $66.40, the stock was approaching its early-October cycle low of $65.08. That level becomes the next downside reference: holding above it would give buyers a chance to stabilize the decline, while a sustained break below would extend the move to a new cycle low.

Housing delivers a clear warning

The most concerning US economic news came from housing. September pending home sales fell 7.3%, far worse than the expected 0.5% decline. The index dropped to a record low of 66.0 from 71.2, with activity down 12.6% from a year earlier.

Pending sales measure signed contracts, so the weakness points to pressure on completed transactions in the months ahead. It also has consequences beyond real estate agents and home sellers. Fewer transactions can mean less spending on furniture, appliances, renovations and moving services.

Housing starts added to the softer picture, coming in at an annualized 1.221 million against expectations of 1.305 million. Building permits offered a better signal at 1.400 million versus 1.395 million expected and 1.275 million previously. That improvement deserves attention, but permission to build does not guarantee that construction will begin quickly.

Taken together, the reports show an interest-rate-sensitive part of the economy struggling. The permits rebound leaves room for improvement, but the collapse in pending sales makes it difficult to dismiss the weakness as noise.

Oil swings as hopes for an Iran deal meet resistance

Oil provided the clearest illustration of the day’s headline risk. Early reports described a compromise proposal from Qatar and Pakistan involving nuclear-site inspections and the release of interest on frozen Iranian funds. That raised hopes for progress and helped push crude down to $95.25.

The move then partly reversed. A subsequent report said talks were continuing but challenged the idea that an agreement was close. Crude recovered above $97 as traders reassessed the likelihood of immediate relief. InvestingLive covered that reversal in its update on the continuing negotiations.

In the later report supplied, WTI was trading at $98.13, down $0.42 on the day but $2.88 above its intraday low. That recovery matters. Oil was lower on the day, but a substantial portion of the earlier relief had disappeared.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described the economy as getting to the other side of the energy shock and said mortgage rates would come down. That is the hopeful outcome. The market still needs sustained evidence. Negotiations can reduce the risk premium quickly, but continued talks are not the same as an agreement that restores confidence in energy supplies.

Ukraine diplomacy adds another potential catalyst

Russia–Ukraine diplomacy also remained in focus. Finland’s President Alexander Stubb described substantive progress toward a peaceful solution, while reports pointed to further US discussions with Russia and the possibility of talks involving Trump, Zelensky and Putin.

President Trump’s later comments emphasized pressure on Ukraine to reach an agreement. He said he wanted Zelensky to make a deal and warned of a bad outcome if Ukraine did not move toward a settlement. InvestingLive’s report on Trump’s comments highlighted the administration’s push for concessions.

For traders, both conflicts present the same challenge: diplomatic progress can move prices before there is a signed agreement. A durable settlement could ease some energy and geopolitical uncertainty. Until the terms and commitments become clearer, the market remains vulnerable to the next headline.

What carries into the next session?

The next test is whether Tuesday’s relief can hold. The dollar moved lower and long-term yields eased, but oil recovered well off its low and the Nasdaq failed to join the stronger Dow and small caps. At the same time, housing supplied a concrete warning about growth.

Traders will be watching whether diplomacy produces something more durable, whether lower long-term yields persist, and whether equity gains broaden into technology. The headlines provided the shove. Now the price action needs to show whether the move has staying power.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

-

SpaceX beat on every line that counts, with AI now its largest business, but a capex bill bigger than its revenue keeps the question of payback firmly on the table.

  • Revenue of about $14.6 billion, up 161% year on year, vs a forecast near $12.9 billion
  • Adjusted EBITDA of about $8.8 billion vs roughly $6.6 billion; operating income of about $2.8 billion vs around $2.2 billion

SpaceX reported third-quarter 2026 results that beat forecasts across revenue, profit and all three business segments, with its AI division now accounting for more than half of total sales.

Earnings per share came in at 35 cents, more than double the 15-cent consensus, while net income of about $4.4 billion compared with expectations near $1.9 billion. Adjusted EBITDA reached about $8.8 billion against a forecast of roughly $6.6 billion, and operating income of about $2.8 billion topped estimates of around $2.2 billion.

The AI segment led the quarter, generating about $7.6 billion in revenue against expectations of $6.3 billion. That puts AI at roughly 52% of group revenue. Connectivity revenue of about $5.3 billion beat the roughly $4.9 billion forecast, and the space segment brought in about $1.8 billion, ahead of estimates near $1.4 billion.

Spending remained heavy. Capital expenditure of about $19.6 billion was in line with forecasts and exceeded the quarter’s total revenue. AI capex made up about $16.4 billion of that, or roughly 84% of the total, and came in slightly below the roughly $16.9 billion analysts had pencilled in. Total costs and expenses of about $11.8 billion ran above the roughly $11.2 billion expected, though strong revenue growth more than absorbed the overrun.

The results suggest the company’s AI investment is producing revenue at a faster pace than analysts had assumed. With quarterly capex still larger than sales, however, the question for investors is how quickly that spending translates into sustainable profit. The gap between costs and estimates will also be worth tracking in coming quarters, particularly if revenue growth moderates from current levels.

item.title: Netflix tops Q3 profit forecast but trims two full-year targets as Q4 guide disappoints
item.description:

A lower free cash flow target tends to weigh on valuation-sensitive growth names, and the shortfall against the roughly $12.6 billion consensus could prompt analysts to revisit full-year models. The read-through for the broader streaming and communication services group may centre on whether spending pressure is building across the sector. Management’s message that internal restructuring is freeing up money for higher-impact areas may help the longer-term case, but it offers little near-term offset to the softer numbers.

-

Netflix delivered a clean third-quarter profit beat, but a weaker Q4 guide and a lower cash flow target shift attention from what it earned to what it plans to spend.

Summary:

  • Q3 EPS of 87 cents beat the 82-cent estimate; revenue of about $12.9 billion matched forecasts
  • Q3 free cash flow of about $2.9 billion missed the roughly $3.2 billion expected
  • Q4 guidance: revenue near $13.4 billion vs about $13.5 billion expected; EPS of 67 cents vs 73 cents; operating margin of 26% vs nearly 28%

  • Full-year free cash flow lowered to about $12 billion from about $12.5 billion, below the roughly $12.6 billion consensus; operating margin target held at 31.5%
  • Management said organizational changes allow it to invest in high-impact areas

Netflix reported third-quarter 2026 earnings that beat forecasts on profit, but its outlook for the final quarter and the full year came in softer than expected, with the company lowering its free cash flow target and guiding fourth-quarter earnings below consensus.

Earnings per share came in at 87 cents, ahead of the 82 cents analysts had expected. Revenue of about $12.9 billion was in line with estimates. Free cash flow for the quarter was a weaker spot, at around $2.9 billion against expectations of roughly $3.2 billion.

The forward guidance is where the results look less comfortable. Netflix said it expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $13.4 billion, slightly below the roughly $13.5 billion forecast. It guided fourth-quarter EPS to 67 cents, short of the 73 cents expected, and operating income to around $3.5 billion against estimates near $3.7 billion. The projected fourth-quarter operating margin of 26% also sits below the nearly 28% consensus.

For the full year, Netflix now expects revenue of about $51.1 billion, at the lower end of its previous $51 billion to $51.4 billion range and a touch under the consensus estimate. Revenue growth guidance narrowed to 13%, from a prior range of 13% to 14%. The full-year operating margin target was held at 31.5%, marginally below the 31.7% analysts had pencilled in.

The largest revision came on cash generation. Netflix lowered its full-year free cash flow forecast to about $12 billion, down from roughly $12.5 billion previously and below the consensus near $12.6 billion.

According to the company, organizational changes are allowing it to direct investment toward high-impact areas. Netflix did not specify those areas in the material provided, but the comment suggests the softer margin and cash flow guidance reflects deliberate spending choices rather than a demand problem, a distinction investors will want tested on the earnings call.

The question for the stock now is whether the market treats the lower targets as a temporary investment phase or as a sign that growth is becoming more expensive to sustain.

item.title: USDCHF consolidates after sharp fall. Traders wait for the next shove.
item.description:
The USDCHF traded to its highest level since May 2025 last Wednesday, reaching 0.83944. However, buyers could not keep the momentum going. The next two trading days saw the price tumble to 0.82162, a decline of nearly 178 pips.

Since Friday’s low, the selling has slowed, but the buyers have not exactly taken control either. The pair has been confined to a narrow trading range, with a ceiling near 0.8274 and a floor near 0.8216. That puts the range at about 58 pips.

A narrow range can remain a narrow range for longer than traders expect. Nevertheless, after the sharp move lower, traders will be watching for a break and run. The technical levels help define where that next shove could develop.

Support is holding, but buyers have work to do

On the downside, the 38.2% retracement of the move up from the August 20 low at 0.8224, together with Friday’s low at 0.82162, defines the key support zone.

Sellers need to get below that area—and stay below—to give the next move lower more credibility. Holding above it keeps the door open for another rotation toward the top of the range.

On the topside, the swing area between 0.8263 and 0.8274 remains the first hurdle. The falling 100-hour moving average at 0.8268 currently sits inside that area, adding another technical reason for sellers to lean against it.

As that moving average continues to fall, its position relative to the swing area will change. For now, the combination gives traders a clear resistance zone. Buyers need to reclaim it to show they can do more than simply defend the lows.

What would a break mean?

A sustained move below 0.8216 would open the door toward 0.8182, followed by the 50% midpoint at 0.81717. Below the midpoint, traders would look toward the 0.8140–0.8150 swing area, followed by the rising 100-day moving average at 0.8127.

On the topside, a break above 0.8274 would give buyers some breathing room, but the falling 200-hour moving average at 0.8297 would quickly become the next test.

Getting above that moving average—and staying above—would strengthen the recovery argument and put the 0.8341–0.8348 swing area in play.

Until those breaks develop, sellers have the sharp decline behind them, while buyers have a floor they continue to defend. The next directional move needs confirmation.

The trading lesson: Let the price confirm the break

When the market is moving sideways, it is easy to anticipate a breakout and get caught in another rotation back across the range.

The better question is: What does the price need to do to confirm my trade, and where would that view be wrong?

For sellers, a break below 0.8216 needs follow-through. A quick move below followed by a rebound above the support zone would be a warning. The sellers would have had their shot. If they cannot keep the price below the floor, some of those sellers may need to buy back.

For buyers, the same logic applies above 0.8274. A break gives them an opportunity, but holding above the broken ceiling—and then tackling the 200-hour moving average—is what would build confidence.

The levels define the risk. The price action tells us whether traders are accepting the break. Until then, respect the range and wait for the next shove.

item.title: BOE's Greene keeps banging the hawkish drum, and she’s not alone anymore
item.description:
• Greene: continue to think we should proactively lean against the risk of second-round inflation effects
  • The risk of second-round effects is greater than we previously thought
  • Wage disinflation looks to have stalled at levels above those consistent with 2% inflation

Megan Greene is sticking to her guns and the message is only getting sharper. Her latest: wage disinflation has stalled at levels inconsistent with 2% inflation, the risk of second-round effects is greater than previously thought, and the BoE should continue to proactively lean against them.

That’s three for three on the hawkish checklist, and nothing we haven’t heard from her before — she’s was one of the three September dissenters voting for a hike to 4%, she warned last week that waiting for second-round effects to show up means acting too late, and she flagged 3.5% pay settlements as a problem on October 8. The November meeting is already priced at 96.7% for a 25 bps hike, so Greene isn’t moving the needle on her own anymore but this may also be a clue that 4.00% won't be enough, nor will be the 5.00% priced in for late 2027.

What strikes me lately is that the IMF meetings produced a noticeable hawkish pivot across the board — officials who had been content to let disinflation run its course came out of Thailand sounding considerably less patient. Supply shocks, sticky services inflation, and wage-setting behavior that refuses to normalize are showing up in speeches from multiple central banks. Greene’s framing — that the asymmetry favors acting early because you can always reverse — is the argument winning the room right now.

For sterling, this isn’t a fresh catalyst. The November hike is baked in and Greene is a known quantity but cable is strong today up 71 pips to 1.3373. What worries me is that the Fed hasn't made the same incrementally hawkish shift since the meeting and that it might show up as a surprise on October 28.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD Technicals: The USDCAD has been trending lower since last Wednesday peak. What next?
item.description:
he USDCAD sellers have been steadily pushing the pair lower since last Wednesday, when the price stalled near the October 9 high. That failure to extend higher gave sellers their opening, and they have taken advantage.

The pair has now declined for four consecutive days. From Wednesday’s high at 1.42984 to today’s low at 1.4033, the price has fallen approximately 265 pips. That is a sizable move in a relatively short period, with a series of broken technical levels giving sellers more confidence along the way.

However, today’s test of the 100-day moving average has attracted some buying interest. The question now is whether buyers can turn that initial response into a larger corrective move.

Sellers have been clearing the downside hurdles

The move lower has seen the USDCAD break below the swing area between 1.41297 and 1.4153, followed by the 38.2% retracement at 1.40818.

Those breaks matter. When a market moves below an established support area and stays below, buyers who leaned against that area are forced to reconsider. At the same time, sellers have another level against which to define their risk on a rebound.

That process has helped keep the downside momentum moving.

Today, the decline reached another important hurdle: the 100-day moving average at 1.4040. The price briefly broke below that level, reaching 1.4033, but could not sustain the break. Instead, buyers pushed the pair back above the moving average.

The sellers had their shot below the 100-day moving average. On the first attempt, they could not keep the price there.

Buyers have a foothold, but there is work to do

The recovery above the 100-day moving average gives buyers a modest technical positive after the sharp decline. It also gives them a nearby reference point for risk.

Stay above 1.4040, and there is room for the corrective move to develop. Move back below—and stay below—and that initial buying response starts to lose its significance.

So far, the rebound has stalled near 1.40566, a prior corrective low from September 23. That level is the first upside hurdle. Getting above it would show buyers are making additional progress, but the more important test comes at the broken 38.2% retracement at 1.40818.

For me, that is the level that would start to make sellers looking for more downside uncomfortable.

A move above 1.40818 would put the price back above a retracement level that helped define the recent bearish move. If buyers can get above and stay above, it would increase the potential for a larger recovery.

The next upside targets would include:

  • 1.41305: The next upside target, near the lower boundary of the broken swing area.
  • 1.4153: The falling 100-hour moving average, which also aligns with the upper boundary of that swing area.

That combination near 1.4153 would make it an important hurdle if the recovery gathers momentum.

A renewed break below 1.4040 keeps sellers in control

Until buyers reclaim those higher levels, the rebound remains a correction within the recent move lower.

A move back below the 100-day moving average at 1.4040 would shift attention to today’s low at 1.4033. Break that low, and the door opens for a test of the 50% midpoint at 1.40149.

Below the midpoint, traders would look toward the 1.3950 area, where the 61.8% retracement of the move higher from the August low is located.

The sellers still have the stronger recent trend. What they need now is confirmation that they can sustain a break below the daily moving average and extend toward those next targets.

Trading lesson: A failed break is a warning. Follow-through determines its importance.

An important lesson here is that a failed break of support can create an opportunity for a rebound, but buyers still need to prove they can take back control.

The recovery above the 100-day moving average tells us that sellers encountered buying interest. It gives traders a clearly defined level to monitor. However, it does not erase the broken support levels overhead or the momentum behind the four-day decline.

Think of the recovery in steps. Holding above 1.4040 is the first step. Getting above 1.40566 is another. Reclaiming 1.40818 would provide stronger evidence that the correction has room to run.

Those steps help traders measure progress and define risk without having to pick the exact bottom.

For now, buyers are making a modest play. Staying above the 100-day moving average keeps that play alive. Getting above 1.40818 would give it more credibility. Until then, sellers have reason to remain confident, but they still need to finish the job below support.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stocks close mostly lower as Middle East headlines drive market swings
item.description:
As London/European traders head for the exits, the major European indices are closing mostly lower. Spain’s Ibex is the exception, while France’s CAC leads the declines.

The closing levels show:

  • Germany’s DAX: down 13.02 points, or 0.05%, at 25,306.76.

  • France’s CAC: down 29.56 points, or 0.38%, at 7,838.50.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: down 31.71 points, or 0.29%, at 10,732.99.

  • Spain’s Ibex: up 53.10 points, or 0.28%, at 19,092.39.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: down 14.92 points, or 0.03%, at 49,071.36.

Middle East headlines keep traders on their toes

The bigger story has been the volatility surrounding the US–Iran negotiations.

Earlier optimism followed an Al Araby Al Jadeed report that Qatar and Pakistan had presented a compromise proposal involving confidential IAEA visits to Iranian nuclear facilities and the release of $6 billion in interest on frozen Iranian funds. The proposal reportedly had US approval and some prior Iranian support, although outstanding differences remained and official confirmation was still needed.

That was enough to trigger a sharp market response. December crude oil, which had traded as high as $101.37, fell to $95.25. US Treasury yields moved lower, stocks received a lift, and the dollar came under pressure.

However, a subsequent report that talks were continuing—but that expectations of an imminent deal were misplaced—took some of the optimism out of the market. Oil rebounded above $97, Treasury yields recovered from their lows, and the dollar clawed back some of its losses.

Separately, Reuters reported that senior Iranian officials described Tehran as deliberately prolonging negotiations, underscoring the obstacles to a quick agreement.

For traders, the distinction matters. Continuing negotiations and reaching an agreement are two different milestones. Prices are reacting to changing probabilities, and each new headline can quickly reverse the previous move.

The GBPUSD provided a good example. Earlier dollar selling pushed the pair above its 100-day moving average at 1.33874. As the optimism faded, the price moved back below that level, bringing last week’s high near 1.3370 back into focus. The headline provided the shove. The technical levels helped measure whether buyers could sustain it.

European yields move lower

European benchmark 10-year yields were lower across the board:

  • Germany:3.397%, down 6.6 basis points.

  • France:4.921%, down 1.8 basis points.

  • UK:5.408%, down 4.2 basis points.

  • Spain:4.028%, down 6.8 basis points.

  • Italy:4.526%, down 6.4 basis points.

European data present an uncomfortable mix

German producer prices rose 1.9% month over month, above the 1.5% estimate and 1.1% previously.

At the same time, confidence weakened. Germany’s ZEW economic sentiment index fell to 28.1, versus 30.2 expected and 34.7 previously. The broader eurozone measure declined to 18.5, below the 23.6 estimate and 25.8 prior reading.

Higher producer prices alongside weaker sentiment create an uncomfortable mix: more inflation pressure at the factory gate, with less confidence in the outlook.

US stocks: Dow leads as tech gains fade

At the supplied market snapshot, US stocks were mixed:

  • Dow industrial average: up 479.05 points, or 0.92%, at 52,450.23.

  • S&P 500: up 23.33 points, or 0.30%, at 7,714.06.

  • Nasdaq 100: down 8.79 points, or 0.03%, at 29,520.55.

The Nasdaq Composite had earlier reached 26,601, highlighting how much of the headline-driven advance had faded. Small caps and the Dow were showing considerably more strength.

US housing disappoints; Treasury curve flattens

US housing starts came in at 1.22 million, below 1.30 million expected. Pending home sales fell 7.3% month over month, much weaker than the 0.6% decline forecast. Building permits were slightly above expectations at 1.40 million, while ADP weekly employment increased 18,500, versus 26,000 previously.

Treasury yields showed longer maturities leading the decline:

  • 5-year:4.918%, down 1.1 basis points.

Oil rebounds; silver and bitcoin advance

The next Middle East headline remains a potential catalyst. Traders have already seen how quickly optimism can build—and how quickly the price action can take some of it back. Stay on your toes.

item.title: GBPUSD Technicals: The price extends gains and moves above the 100 day MA in the process
item.description:
GBPUSD breaks above its 100-day moving average as Iran headlines pressure the dollar

The GBPUSD is pushing to new highs for the day as reports of a potential compromise between the US and Iran send oil prices and US yields lower, while putting pressure on the dollar.

According to Al Araby Al Jadeed, Qatar and Pakistan have presented a proposal that includes a secret IAEA visit to Iranian nuclear sites and the release of $6 billion in interest on frozen Iranian funds. The proposal reportedly has US approval and some prior Iranian support, although differences remain and official confirmation is still needed.

The market is responding to the prospect of reduced tensions. December crude oil futures have fallen below $96 after trading above $101 earlier. Meanwhile, the US 10-year yield is down 4.6 basis points to 5.089%, moving further away from last week’s high near 5.36%.

Lower oil prices could ease some inflation concerns, while falling US yields reduce the dollar’s interest-rate support. The GBPUSD has been the biggest mover, with buyers pushing the pair above its 100-day moving average for the first time since September 16. Remember, a higher GBPUSD means a stronger pound relative to the dollar—and a weaker dollar relative to the pound.

The headlines provide the catalyst. The technicals define the next steps.

The break above the 100-day moving average at 1.33875 is a positive development for buyers. Staying above that level would be the best-case scenario for keeping the upside momentum intact.

However, the price is moving into an area where buyers have more work to do:

  • 1.33875: The 100-day moving average and the first support level following the break.

  • 1.34056: The 50% midpoint of the decline from the August 2026 high to last week’s low at 1.3136.

  • 1.34314: The 200-day moving average and the next major topside hurdle.

Today’s high has reached 1.3409, taking the price just above the 50% midpoint. Buyers have cleared that level briefly. Now they need to show they can stay above it and build toward the 200-day moving average.

The midpoint matters because it divides the prior decline in half. Getting above it means buyers have recovered more than half of that move lower. Holding above it would strengthen the recovery story.

Why sellers may lean against this area

Even with the bullish momentum, a rally into major technical levels can attract selling.

Traders who bought earlier at lower levels may take some profit. Sellers may also lean against resistance because the levels give them a reference point for defining and limiting risk. If the price breaks above their chosen resistance level and stays above it, the reason for the trade weakens.

That does not guarantee a reversal. It explains why the rally could slow as the price works through the midpoint and toward the 200-day moving average.

What would weaken the bullish move?

The first test is whether buyers can hold above 1.33875. A move back below the 100-day moving average would take some shine off the breakout and shift attention to 1.3371, Friday’s high and last week’s high.

I would not want to see the price move below that level on a correction. A break above last week’s high followed by a move back below it would suggest buyers are struggling to sustain the breakout. That could lead to some unraveling of today’s bullish momentum.

The buyers have made an important move. Now they need to defend it. Stay above the 100-day moving average, and buyers retain the stronger position. Get above—and stay above—the midpoint and then the 200-day moving average, and the bullish story gains further confirmation.
